scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9007: Hello IT, the partner connection keeps HICCUPING -- pc2
at 200.1.1.2 drops out on me every so often and feels slow in between. I'm on
pc1. Something around the link between our border router and theirs must be
going wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone look at it and make it stay
up for more than five minutes!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. The
  peering is stable and reachability is loss-free. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of an intermittent/flap
  symptom that is not occurring -- does the agent check session stability and
  loss against the live network, or confabulate a flapping peering?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- a flapping/slow peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1 (195.11.14.2)
reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and stable low latency, the router1<->router2
eBGP session is Established with a steady uptime (not resetting), and no route
churn is observed.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the peering is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent checks the BGP
session state/uptime on router1 and router2 and runs a sustained ping pc1->pc2,
finds them stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring the peering flapping or resetting router1/router2's BGP to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The reported symptom — intermittent drops and slowness on the pc1-to-pc2 path via the inter-router link — is unconfirmed by direct evidence. A complete diagnostic pass across all layers found nothing injecting the reported behavior.

Layer 2 and addressing (Phase A): infra_sweep flagged zero devices; no ACL rules, no static ARP, no misconfigured gateways or resolvers on either host. l2_snapshot found only all-zero MACs on standard Linux tunnel interfaces (gre0, sit0, etc.), which are kernel artifacts present on all devices equally — not a conflict.

Control plane and traffic shaping (Phase B): bgp_snapshot shows both router1 (AS 1) and router2 (AS 2) with BGP fully established, correct prefix advertisements, and symmetric routing tables. tc_snapshot confirms all six interfaces run default pfifo_fast with no shaping, policing, or delay qdiscs.

Resource pressure (Phase D): pressure_sweep found no stress tools, no CPU spikes, no socket exhaustion on any device.

BGP session history: the FRR log on both routers covers the entire session lifecycle from startup (04:58:21). The log records a single one-time connection-collision resolution during simultaneous TCP open — a normal eBGP startup event — followed by steady 60-second keepalive exchanges with no session resets, no NOTIFICATION messages due to hold-timer expiry, and no route withdrawals. Carrier counters on router1 and router2 eth0 show zero errors and zero drops. Cron jobs on both routers are standard system maintenance only; there are no network-disruption scripts.

Root cause: no fault is present in this topology; the reported intermittent drops have no corresponding mechanism or historical trace in the live network.

Fix: none required. If the user observes further disruption, capture a ping log with timestamps; the current snapshot and full session history show a stable, correctly configured eBGP topology.
